item.title: Taveuni water shortage forces resident to pay $792 for 20,000 litres
item.description: As dry weather conditions continue to affect water supply in parts of Taveuni, a resident was charged about 15 times more for 20,000 litres of water, with the Water Authority of Fiji saying the amount included transportation and delivery costs, while an earlier $53 charge was for the water only. item.content:encoded:
As dry weather conditions continue to affect water supply in parts of Taveuni, a resident was charged about 15 times more for 20,000 litres of water, with the Water Authority of Fiji saying the amount included transportation and delivery costs, while an earlier $53 charge was for the water only.

The resident raised concerns about the significant difference between the two charges and says he is still waiting for 10,000 litres of the water he paid $792 for on 12th August.

This comes as residents in parts of Taveuni continue to face water supply issues, due to dry weather conditions.

The resident, who also runs a business, says the ongoing supply problems have forced him to pay for water to be delivered to meet his needs.

He says some water usually comes through in the morning, but the pressure is low, and by around lunchtime there is often no water supply at all.

The resident says the unreliable supply is why he had to order 20,000 litres of water from WAF and pay for it to be delivered.

WAF says water costs $26.50 per 5,000 litres, meaning a customer who arranges their own transport would pay $53 for 10,000 litres.

They says residents can use their own trucks, tanks or private transport to collect water from a WAF-approved source and would only be charged for the water.

However, WAF says additional charges apply when the Authority arranges transportation and delivery, with the cost depending on the distance.

They says the Taveuni resident's location falls under Category C, which covers a distance of 21 to 30 kilometres.

Under this category, WAF says ea ch 5,000-litre delivery costs $198, including the water and transportation.

They sa y four trips using a 5,000-litre truck are required to deliver 20,000 litres, bringing the total cost to $792.

However, the resident says he paid the full $792 on 12th August and has so far received only two deliveries, totalling 10,000 litres.

WAF confirms that two trips were initially made but says their Taveuni staff were told by the resident that he would contact them when he was ready to receive the remaining 10,000 litres.

The resident, however, says he has since made several attempts to contact the WAF team about the remaining water but has not received a response.

WAF maintains that its team is waiting for the resident to contact them so arrangements can be made to deliver the remaining 10,000 litres.

The Authority also confirms that water used for its carting service in Taveuni is sourced from the Waiyevo Filling Point.

WAF says water cart tanks are inspected and flushed daily, while its laboratory team carries out safety tests on water cart trucks every three months.

They says all water supplied through WAF is fully treated.

item.title: Special fijivillage Straight Talk Public Forum on Online Safety to be held at 7pm Friday September 4th
item.description: A special fijivillage Straight Talk Public Forum with Vijay Narayan will go live at 7pm Friday September 4th. The theme of the forum is Online Safety: Connected and Protected?
item.content:encoded:
A special fijivillage Straight Talk Public Forum with Vijay Narayan will go live at 7pm Friday September 4th.

The theme of the forum is Online Safety: Connected and Protected?

The panelists for the public forum will be Online Safety Commissioner, Filipe Barisal, Fiji Law Reform Commissioners David Solvalu and Valerie Narain.

The Straight Talk forum will focus on Online Safety Issues in Fiji, what is being faced by the Online Safety Commission, the feedback from the members of the public during the consultation process on the review of the Online Safety Act 2018, the call for age restrictions for Social Media, the response from victims, the changes being proposed and the reasons behind them amongst other issues.

You can also be part of the live audience by applying for registration with a question that you would like to ask during the forum.

The application to register details can be found on our website and facebook page, fijivillage.

You will receive a confirmation if you have been selected to be part of the live audience.

Please apply early to avoid any disappointment.

The show will be broadcast live at 7pm Friday September 4th on our Facebook, YouTube and X.

item.title: 3 remanded for alleged robbery of Nadi taxi driver
item.description: Rashika Kumar , Vijay Narayan · 28/08/2026 The three people who allegedly robbed a Nadi taxi driver on Tuesday morning have been remanded by the Nadi Magistrates Court.
item.content:encoded:
Rashika Kumar , Vijay Narayan · 28/08/2026

The three people who allegedly robbed a Nadi taxi driver on Tuesday morning have been remanded by the Nadi Magistrates Court.

Iliesa Buka, Serupepeli Bogisa and Livai Nakacia have been charged with aggravated robbery and appeared in the Nadi Magistrates Court this afternoon.

Police confirm that the fourth suspect remains in custody.

The first suspect surrendered to Police after a video of the incident went viral on social media.

Police took two more suspects in for questioning on Wednesday morning, while the fourth suspect surrendered to Police at the Vatuwaqa Police Post on Wednesday night.

The matter will now be called in the Lautoka High Court on 11th September.

item.title: New shelter opens in West for women and girls affected by violence, drugs and trafficking
item.description: Women and girls escaping gender-based violence in the Western Division will have access to safe accommodation, counselling and other support services through a new Women's Safe Shelter opening from Monday. The shelter will provide emergency accommodation for survivors of gender-based violence, as well as trauma-informed counselling, social work support, case management and referrals to other servi
item.content:encoded:
Women and girls escaping gender-based violence in the Western Division will have access to safe accommodation, counselling and other support services through a new Women's Safe Shelter opening from Monday.

The shelter will provide emergency accommodation for survivors of gender-based violence, as well as trauma-informed counselling, social work support, case management and referrals to other services.

The location of the shelter is being kept confidential, to protect the safety and privacy of women and girls who will use the facility.

While opening the shelter in Lautoka, Minister for Women and Children Sashi Kiran says the need for such facilities is changing as Fiji faces wider challenges affecting women and children, including drugs and trafficking.

She says during a recent street sweep in the Western Division, authorities found a 16-year-old pregnant girl who had been living on the streets.

Kiran says the girl, who is close to giving birth, is now in the Ministry's care but has not been able to return to her family.

She says authorities are also seeing girls as young as 13, 14 and 15 becoming pregnant and being drawn into situations involving drugs and trafficking.

Kiran says these cases are deeply concerning and greater attention needs to be placed on parenting and the role families and communities play in protecting children.

She says while shelters may have previously focused mainly on domestic violence, services now need to respond to increasingly complex situations involving children affected by drugs, parents using drugs and young people being pushed or lured into harmful situations.

Kiran says greater attention must also be given to girls affected by drug addiction and trafficking while more comprehensive support services are being developed.

She says children are among the most vulnerable members of society, and families, communities and organisations need to strengthen the protection and support available to them.

The organisation operating the shelter Empower Pacific, says it will provide women and girls with a safe environment where they can recover with dignity and be involved in decisions about their future.

They will also work with government agencies, non-government organisations, faith-based groups, the private sector and other organisations to provide further support to survivors.

item.title: Tuvaluans moved to tears by film revisiting Nukulaelae blackbirding
item.description: A film revisiting the removal of about 80 percent of Nukulaelae's population for forced labour in 1863, has left some audience members in Tuvalu shocked and in tears. The Stolen Laevans of Tuvalu: The Peruvian Slavery Nightmare was co-produced by the University of Fiji and the Kaupule of Nukulaelae and premiered during the Fakaapo-Tuvalu Arts Festival earlier this week.
item.content:encoded:
A film revisiting the removal of about 80 percent of Nukulaelae's population for forced labour in 1863, has left some audience members in Tuvalu shocked and in tears.

The Stolen Laevans of Tuvalu: The Peruvian Slavery Nightmare was co-produced by the University of Fiji and the Kaupule of Nukulaelae and premiered during the Fakaapo-Tuvalu Arts Festival earlier this week.

The film revisits the blackbirding of Nukulaelae, when people were taken by slave vessels and forced to work in guano mines and plantations in Peru.

University of Fiji Head of Corporate Services Seve Paeniu says the premiere attracted a large audience, with some people visibly shaken by what their ancestors had endured.

Paeniu says the film has strongly connected with Tuvaluans and will help ensure their ancestors and their experiences are not forgotten.

Tuvalu Prime Minister Feleti Teo says the film is a powerful reminder of the injustices suffered by the people of Nukulaelae.

Teo says some form of reparation or compensation could be considered, and his government is ready to support efforts to promote the messages highlighted in the film.

The documentary also focuses on the resilience of later generations and draws a connection between the history of displacement and challenges facing Tuvalu today, including climate change, rising sea levels and the possibility of communities being displaced.

University of Fiji Vice-Chancellor Professor Shaista Shameem says the documentary was developed through the University's Journalism and Media Studies Documentary course after lecturers learnt about the history of the slave trade in Tuvalu.

She says lecturers and students carried out further research before developing the story into a documentary for an international audience.

The film will have its Fiji premiere in September before being taken to international film festivals.

The University says the project aims to preserve an important part of Tuvalu and Pacific history, ensure the experiences of those affected are not forgotten, and encourage wider discussions about blackbirding and restorative justice.
